title: Lack of COP31 agreement 'deeply disappointing' Environment Minister says
transcript:
Host:
And to federal politics now, and a climate and energy Minister Chris Bowen says progress has been made at the COP 31 summit in Tuquia, despite countries walking away without any agreement. Negotiations led by the Australian delegation collapsed overnight after a host of nations led by Europe uh bulked at a draft that didn't mention phasing out of fossil fuels. Earlier this morning, I spoke to Bill Hare, an Australian climate scientist and former lead author of the intergovernmental panel on climate change.
Speaker 2:
I think there was a lot of countries that needed to see a transition away from fossil fuels. They didn't want to have this horrible language on carbon capture and storage. They didn't want to see the weakening of climate science, and that's what came through in the last 48 hours in the presidency text.
Host:
That's Bill Hare speaking there. Well, Mary Watt is the Federal Minister for Environment and Water and joins me now in our Parliament House Studio. A Minister, welcome back.
Mary Watt:
Good day, Sally. Good to be here.
Host:
Is this a failure at COP 31?
Mary Watt:
No, I don't think it is. It's obviously a very deeply disappointing outcome uh that the cover decision was not uh agreed to by all nations. My understanding is that there were close to 90 nations who were prepared to support that cover decision, and that includes everyone from China and India, Pakistan, Canada through to some of the Pacific nations like Fiji and Palau. Uh but obviously uh agreement was not able to be reached across what are some very divergent interests. You know, I think what this shows, it's a very challenging international environment at the moment to reach agreement on almost anything. Uh and particularly a situation like this where you've got fossil fuel producers on the one hand and other countries that are experiencing very serious impacts from climate change. That's a very wide bridge uh to be uh a very wide divide to be breached uh and and it's very disappointing that that wasn't possible.
Host:
Does Australia bear responsibility as head of the negotiations for this failure to to reach consensus?
Mary Watt:
No, I mean my impression is that Chris Bowen, as the president of the negotiations, put in an enormous effort both before, during, and during the COP. I heard the interview with Bill Hare earlier today, uh and you know, he's obviously someone with very strong opinions on these matters, and he acknowledged the enormous effort that Chris put in uh to get this agreement over the line. Uh whether it's Chris or anyone else, if you're a negotiator and you've got different parties who are incredibly far apart, it is very difficult to be able to bridge that divide. Uh I don't think it's But agreement has been reached at previous COPs. It's not impossible.
Mary Watt:
It has, and again, I think that shows the very difficult state of international affairs at the moment. Uh you know, we the US did not send an official delegate delegation to this COP. Uh we've got obviously other fossil fuel producing countries who've got very firm positions, other countries on the other side of the debate with very firm positions as well. Uh I I think it would be very challenging for anyone to be able to bridge that divide. Having said that, you know, I think it's important to recognize that uh while the cover decision was not agreed, there were 44 of 60 substantive items before the conference where consensus was reached, and that includes support to be provided to working people uh as we move towards clean energy. uh and Chris and the Australian government was able to negotiate very important agreements with countries like Korea and Denmark to attract more renewable energy investment here. So, there is some there are some positives that have come out of this, but I recognize that it's a disappointing outcome overall.
Host:
Australia's lead of the negotiations. This has been a lot of money, uh a lot of time, and a lot of uh effort. In retrospect, was it not a good idea to pursue this leadership of the negotiations?
Mary Watt:
No, I think it's always important for Australia to play a leading role in international negotiations that are likely to have impacts on Australia. The best way that we can promote Australia's national interest internationally is by playing a leading role in those negotiations, whatever they're about. Uh, you know, I'm I know the opposition would like to say that this is a waste of time. We should just stay at home and ignore these kind of things. That's a sure-fire way to ensure that we get left behind by the rest of the world. We saw what that approach did uh under 10 years of coalition government, where we became an international pariah on these issues. We lost the confidence of the Pacific, the the region that is most important to us strategically. Uh so there are there are a range of reasons for us to pursue these sorts of negotiations and it but it is disappointing that we weren't able to get there.
Host:
Why was the language on fossil fuels not included?
Mary Watt:
Uh, well, again, I'm I'm going off what's been reported, uh but uh it it appears clear that there were a range of nations that were simply not prepared to sign up to an agreement that included those words. Uh, equally, there were clearly nations that would only sign up if those words were present. And this is the difficulty you've got when you've got different groups uh taking very, very different positions. Sometimes it can be very hard to reconcile them. I think it's worth noting that uh I think it was COP 28 in Dubai where there was previously a decision made uh to transition away from fossil fuels, so that is a decision already made by COP. The focus of this conference was about how we would get there, uh but clearly though, those issues remain very important for a number of countries.
Host:
What's the message does that send to Australia's Pacific partners? A part of the reason of going for the leadership of COP was to represent the Pacific family. If Australia can't get language in about fossil fuels, what's the point?
Mary Watt:
Well, we can only achieve uh what other countries are prepared to agree to. Uh we didn't have some veto power or some ability to decide on behalf of the rest of the world what would go in the text of that cover decision. It's a negotiation. Uh and I know, uh and from my personal experience with Chris Bowen that he will have put every ounce of blood that he could have into convincing nations to come to an agreement. Uh we're all aware that the conference has gone a couple of days over time in order to try to reach that agreement, but ultimately that was not possible. Can I just say one other thing about the attacks from the opposition on this uh Sally. I've noticed already this morning they've been making the argument that we shouldn't even bother with these kind of conferences, all we should be focused on is affordable energy. Well, the opposition have got an ability this week in Parliament to support cheaper energy by backing in the government's domestic gas reservation. If they're serious about this, rather than just having political lines, they will back that uh legislation.
Host:
Well, let's talk about gas reservation. The coalition says it supports the scheme in principle in the government's view. What's stopping the two major parties coming to an agreement? Or do you now think that the Greens are the most likely option to get it through?
Mary Watt:
Well, of course, we have to keep both options open, Sally, because we're absolutely determined to pass this legislation, to make sure that Australians have cheaper energy. Uh, you know, it's important to Australian households, it's important to Australian industry, that we reduce the price of gas. And one of the ways that we can do that is by making sure that Australians keep more Australian produced gas. It is absolutely absurd that in a country like Australia that produces a large amount of gas, uh that we face rising prices and at times the risk of shortfalls. The way we can solve that is to reserve up to 20% of our gas exports for exports for Australians. This is Australian gas, it belongs to Australians. Australians should benefit from that gas in the form of cheaper gas, and now we need one of those parties, the coalition or the Greens to recognize that and come to the party.
Host:
Are you leaning one way or the other?
Mary Watt:
No, I mean I'm not personally directly involved in these negotiations, Sally, uh but uh clearly the ministers responsible have been negotiating with both sides. Uh, you know, I think uh up and up until last week, we certainly felt that the coalition was the more likely party, but we're we're seeing the same kind of intransigence from them that we saw last year with the EPBC reforms. Um, but this week is an important week and this is the week that the coalition can decide if they support cheaper gas.
Host:
Have you been done this week?
Mary Watt:
That's certainly the intention. I think it's also worth noting one other group that has evaded scrutiny on this is uh Pauline Hanson's One Nation Party. Uh, they have traditionally supported a gas reservation, uh, but mysteriously shortly after uh, Gina Reinhardt, who's a big gas producer has supported their party, they flip their position. I think it would be very interesting to Australians to understand why they no longer support a gas reservation when they always have before.
Host:
Mary Watt, we'll need to leave it there. Thank you for coming in this morning.
Mary Watt:
Thanks, Sally.
